claim: Along the constant-oxygen-partial-pressure (normoxic) cabin band, silicone (MQ), nylon 6,6 (PA-66) and fluoroelastomer (FKM) are non-flammable only at pressures above a normoxic upward limiting pressure of up to 101.3 kPa, so they become flammable in lower-pressure, higher-oxygen cabin atmospheres.
quote: Where the material crosses the upper limit of the spacecraft normoxic control band (±2% on the fixed partial pressure of oxygen) can be considered the Normoxic Upward Limiting Pressure (NULP). At pressures above this, the material is not flammable. In Figure 7, all three green line materials (MQ, PA-66, FKM) have NULP values of up to 101.3 kPa.

limits: The authors re-plotted earlier WSTF MOC data (Hirsch et al.) for 11 different spacecraft materials in Figure 7; these are not new measurements. 1 g, quiescent, Test 1 only. 'Up to 101.3 kPa' is an upper bound, not an exact per-material value; the paper suggests adding a safety factor of about 10 kPa. The same text says PTFE and PCTFE are not flammable in any spacecraft normoxic atmosphere and six other materials are flammable in all of them.

verifier_note: Quote exact (PDF p.9). claim: NASA White Sands researchers conclude that flammability data from 21% oxygen at 101.4 kPa cannot be conservatively applied to higher-oxygen, lower-pressure atmospheres such as 30% oxygen at 70.3 kPa, even when the oxygen partial pressure is equal.
quote: The conclusion drawn from these data is that lower concentration/higher pressure data (e.g., 21% O2, 101.4 kPa (14.7 psia)) cannot be conservatively applied to higher oxygen concentration/lower pressure environments (e.g., 30%, 70.3 kPa (10.2 psia)) despite equivalent partial pressures.

limits: Presentation slides, not a test report. The probability figures are labelled '1993-2004 round robin history'; the slide gives neither the number of tests nor the atmosphere for them. M22759 is a wire specification family; insulation polymer and gauge are not given. On the 2006 data slide (JAXA, MSFC, WSTF; five specimens each) burn lengths range from 3.8 to 29.7 cm. Olson et al. 2014 (NTRS 20150004099) report that 16 of 30 tests failed Test 4 for this wire at 30% O2, 10.2 psia. NASA JSC 29353B says most aerospace-grade wire insulation is nonflammable in ISS and exploration environments, so this is one wire type, not all wire. The same deck reports a 2.8% per-sample failure probability for M81044 wire at 20.9% O2, 14.7 psia.
